title: Power method for the top eigenvector

sections.body_md:
The power method finds a dominant eigenvector of a symmetric matrix by repeating one multiplication. Start with a nonzero vector that is not orthogonal to the top eigenvector, multiply by the matrix, and divide by the Euclidean length. The same normalization is what the conditional-gradient oracle returns for the objective \(x^T A x\) on the unit sphere: the gradient points along \(A x\), and the linear maximizer on the sphere is the normalization of \(A x\).

Write the start in an orthonormal eigenbasis. Multiplication by \(A\) multiplies the coefficient of each eigenvector by its eigenvalue. Dividing by the length does not change the ratios of those coefficients. If the top eigenvalue is strictly larger in magnitude than the second, the top coefficient pulls ahead. The ratio of the second coefficient to the first is multiplied by \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|\) at every step. That factor governs the angle between the iterate and the top eigenvector.

The Rayleigh quotient is a different error. On a unit vector the weight on a stray mode is the square of that mode's coefficient, so the gap from \(\lambda_1\) scales with the square of \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|\). Quoting the unsquared factor as a Rayleigh error mixes the two measures.

A start orthogonal to the top eigenvector never grows that component. Applying the same iteration to \(A^T A\) approaches a top right singular vector of \(A\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
One step is
\[
x_+ = \frac{A x}{\lVert A x\rVert}.
\]
If \(|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2|\), the second-mode coefficient is multiplied by \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|\) at each step. The Rayleigh gap from \(\lambda_1\) scales with the square of that factor. The Rayleigh quotient itself is \(x^T A x / x^T x\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(A = \mathrm{diag}(8,\ 2)\) and the start \((1,\ 1)\). One multiplication produces \((8,\ 2)\). The ratio of the second component to the first falls from \(1\) to \(2/8\).

The mast ratio is 0.25, which is \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1| = 2/8\). A second multiplication produces \((64,\ 4)\), and the component ratio is \(1/16\). The Rayleigh gap of a tiny second component \(\varepsilon\) moves like \(\varepsilon^2\), so one step multiplies that gap by \((1/4)^2\).

The quotient of \((8,\ 2)\) is \(520/68\), strictly below the top eigenvalue \(8\). The component ratio \(0.25\) is not that gap.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The factor \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|\) multiplies a mode coefficient and governs an angle. Using it, unsquared, as the Rayleigh error overstates how fast the eigenvalue estimate improves, because the quotient sees the square. A second slip is to invert the factor. \(|\lambda_1 / \lambda_2|\) is larger than one and would describe a growing component. A third is to start in the lower eigenspace and expect the top direction to appear. Multiplication cannot create a missing component. One step is not an exact eigenvector unless the start was already aligned. The contraction is geometric.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Power iteration on \(A^T A\) is the same algorithm pointed at a top right singular vector. The angle contracts by the ratio of the two largest eigenvalues of that product, the squares of the two largest singular values. The Rayleigh quotient of \(A^T A\) estimates a squared singular value and converges with the square of the angle factor.
